 What we're watching
 Game 4 is here : The Milwaukee Brewers are one win away from the franchise’s first World Series title. After a massive 10-1 win Monday, the Brewers hold a dominant 3-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays .
 Milwaukee answers again: Tampa took the lead to start the game and Milwaukee answered in the top of the fourth. The Rays immediately retook the lead and the Brewers promptly scored again to tie it up. It’s 2-2 in the sixth.
 Tampa Bay faces long odds : Twenty-five previous teams have gone down 0-3 in a World Series. None of them have come back to win. That’s the task that the Rays face tonight.
 History predicts a sweep: Of the 25 previous teams to take a 3-0 World Series lead, 21 of them have won Game 4 to sweep the series. The Brewers hope to make it 22 tonight.

 Rays turn to Game 1 starter Nick Martinez in relief
 By Kevin Dotson 
 Tampa Bay's Nick Martinez pitches the sixth inning. 
 Jamie Squire/Getty Images 
 Desperate times call for desperate measures. Enter Nick Martinez – the Rays’ scheduled Game 5 starting pitcher.
 After a strong outing as the starter in Game 1, Martinez looked up to the pressure of the moment in his first inning of relief, retiring the Brewers in a scoreless sixth inning marred only by a bloop single from Cooper Pratt.
 As for tomorrow? The Rays will cross that bridge when (if?) they come to it.
 Score: Rays 2, Brewers 2

 MLB's Stand Up To Cancer moment pulls at the heartstrings
 By Kyle Feldscher 
 It’s an annual tradition that means a lot to many – the Game 4 moment in which players and fans of both teams unite, along with nearly everyone else in the stadium, to remember those lost to cancer.
 The pause in the game is powerful and provides a soft moment to remember all those affected by such a terrible disease.

 Brewers bringing in the big guns: Their unbeatable bullpen
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Brewers reliever Abner Uribe throws a pitch in the fifth inning. 
 Mike Stobe/Getty Images 
 Pat Murphy, confident in his team’s ability to make a comeback, is going to his high-leverage arms already.
 Abner Uribe comes out of the ‘pen and gets a pair of strikeouts and a soft ground out to sit down the bottom of the order in, well, order.
 The game is still tied but that frame made it feel like Milwaukee is in control. Their bullpen – this month especially – is a force to behold.
 If the Rays are going to live to play another day, they’ll have to get something going against a relief corps with a 1.34 ERA this postseason.

 We're halfway home and Game 4 is tied 2-2

 Milwaukee's David Hamilton rounds the bases after his fifth-inning home run tied the game.

 After a gutsy performance from starting pitcher Griffin Jax, Rays manager Kevin Cash handed the ball over to high-leverage reliever Kevin Kelly.
 Kelly made quick work of the rest of the fifth inning, pitching around a two-out walk of Christian Yelich to preserve the tie score as Game 5 reached the midway point.

 Rays take the lead on aggressive base running and Brewers' error
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero avoids a tag attempt from David Hamilton just before scoring. 
 Mike Stobe/Getty Images 
 This World Series has not lacked for action on the basepaths. This time, it’s the Rays who benefit from a blunder by the Brewers.
 A leadoff single from Junior Caminero on the first pitch of the frame ends Dustin Mays’ night. Against JoJo Romero, Liam Hicks moves Caminero to second on a ground out. So far pretty straightforward.
 OK so. Caminero on second. Jonny DeLuca hits a ball to Brewers third baseman David Hamilton, who tries to tag Caminero running by.
 David Hamilton wasn't able to make the tag on Junior Caminero and he ends up scoring after the throwing error to give the Rays the lead in the 4th pic.twitter.com/oJ44uIfWVb 
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 28, 2026 
 Caminero evades the tag and Hamilton throws the ball away trying to get the out at first base. Caminero comes around to score.
 Brewers challenge, alleging Hamilton got Caminero but the call is upheld. The Rays go ahead.
 But that’s right where the Brewers want ‘em.
 Score: Rays 2, Brewers 1

 Why baseball teams party so hard and so often in October
 By Don Riddell 
 The Milwaukee Brewers celebrate after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers to win the National League Championship Series. 
 Ashley Landis/AP 
 At the end of this series, the final party will begin. It will be the last in a long line of them.
 Every major US sport has multi-round postseason schedules, but none of them party like MLB teams. Locker room celebrations in the NFL tend to be subdued until the Super Bowl, and since hockey players are famously superstitious, popping bottles early is practically verboten in the NHL; the Stanley Cup is all that really matters.
 Boston Red Sox clubhouse manager Tom McLaughlin has spent over 40 years with the Red Sox, and he says he’s lost track of how many celebrations he’s been involved in, but he counts them in the dozens. He told CNN Sports it was “pretty tame” when he started in the ‘80s, when the postseason was much shorter, but the back end of the season now can feel like one enormous bender for the most successful teams.
 Clinched a playoff spot? Party.
 Successfully navigate the wildcard round? Let’s get wild.
 Made it through the Divisional Round? Get another round in.
 Won the Championship Series? We’re going on a spree.
 By the time a baseball club wins the World Series , let’s just say that the celebration will not be their first rodeo. Everyone will have had plenty of practice.
 Read more here on why baseball teams party all the time, party all the time, party all the time in October.

 Brewers tie the game with more clutch 2-out hitting
 By Kevin Dotson 
 Rays outfielder Jonny DeLuca catches a fly ball in the fourth inning. 
 Chris O'Meara/AP 
 The fourth inning started with another big play from the Rays as center fielder Jonny DeLuca robbed William Contreras with a fabulous diving catch that could have been big trouble if it had gotten past him.
 Griffin Jax then notched his fifth K of the game with a three-pitch strikeout of Brice Turang.
 But like last night’s Game 3, the Brewers found some two-out lighting with a single from Sal Frelick quickly followed by a double from Cooper Pratt to score Frelick and tie the game.
 Cooper Pratt drives in Sal Frelick to tie it up in Game 4! pic.twitter.com/OHFzAwNc4w 
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 28, 2026 
 Jax bounced back with a strikeout of Garrett Mitchell to end the inning with no further damage.
 Score: Brewers 1, Rays 1

 Rays return to their not-hitting ways
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Strikeout, ground out, fly out from Taylor Walls, Yandy Díaz, and Jonathan Aranda, respectively.
 The Rays are showing range in how they make outs, but the end result is yet another 1-2-3 inning.
 Sure, they still lead in the game, but we’ve written some version of that an awful lot this series. Entering tonight, the Rays lineup was hitting just .187 in the Fall Classic.

 Jax continues to hold the Brewers at bay
 By Kevin Dotson 
 Griffin Jax struck out David Hamilton swinging to open the third inning and complete one scoreless trip through the Brewers’ dangerous lineup.
 Jackson Chourio gave a rude welcome to the second time around with a single into right field, Chourio’s ninth hit of the World Series.
 Next up, Jake Bauers gave Jax a scare with a ball deep into left-center field, but speedy center fielder Jonny DeLuca was able to track it down and haul in the catch before running into the wall.
 Jax ended the inning with a check-swing strikeout of Christian Yelich.

 A couple of speedsters combine for Rays' first run
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca scores the first run of Game 4. 
 Ashley Landis/AP 
 The Rays have a lead and a little life left!
 So far this World Series, we’ve talked a lot about what the Brewers do well and what the Rays had done well previously but lately have been struggling with. Here’s something Tampa has done consistently well: Run really fast.
 Jonny DeLuca (94th percentile sprint speed) reaches first based on a fielder’s choice and then scores on a double from Chandler Simpson (95th percentile sprint speed). Speed puts pressure on the opposition and finally, that’s translating to scoring for Tampa Bay.

 Rays starter Griffin Jax continued to pitch like he had nothing to lose in the second inning.
 Pitching to contact, Jax induced a pair of hard-hit lineouts to the outfield from Sal Frelick and Cooper Pratt.
 Jax put a cherry on top of another scoreless inning with a strikeout of Garrett Mitchell.

 Rays' do-or-die game off to inauspicious start
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Rays third baseman Junior Caminero walks to the dugout after striking out in the first inning. 
 Ashley Landis/AP 
 The Rays presumably came back tonight looking to atone for was not just a loss, but an embarrassing beat down. Surely they are motivated, prideful, and frankly, desperate.
 So it’s a little disconcerting that the first inning in a do-or-die game consisted of a throwing error in the top half and a quiet 1-2-3 frame in the bottom.
 Junior Caminero, the heart of their lineup and their best offensive force, struck out looking to end the inning,
 PAINT by Dustin May to strikeout Junior Caminero for a 1-2-3 first inning pic.twitter.com/1xtVG5z8L7

 It was an inauspicious start.

 Rays allow a couple walks but escape trouble in the first
 By Kevin Dotson 
 Rays starter Griffin Jax walked a couple of batters in the first inning but got out of it unscathed. 
 Carmen Mandato/Getty Images 
 With the weight of the world (or at least the Tampa Bay area) on his shoulders, Rays starting pitcher Griffin Jax appears to be attempting a novel approach: Pounding the strike zone. At least to start.
 His aggression yielded quick results, as Jax struck out Jackson Chourio and got a quick flyout from Jake Bauers.
 Jax took a more cautious approach against Brewers captain Christian Yelich, walking him on four pitches.
 Yelich then stole second and took third on an errant throw from Tampa Bay catcher Liam Hicks. Jax then, perhaps wisely, issued a walk to the red-hot William Contreras.
 Jax escaped unscathed by inducing an inning-ending groundout to shortstop from Brice Turang.
 Griffin Jax gets out of the jam in the first to keep the Brewers off the board pic.twitter.com/pzaht4tN4F 
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 28, 2026 
 Any scoreless inning against this Brewers lineup has to feel like a moral victory for the Rays.
 Score: Brewers 0, Rays 0

 Brewers fans turning Tampa into Milwaukee south
 By Kevin Dotson 
 A Brewers fan wears a cheesehead hat while watching warmups before Game 4. 
 Chris O'Meara/AP 
 From the sounds of it, title-starved Milwaukee Brewers fans are making themselves right at home at St. Petersburg’s Tropicana Field.
 The Brew Crew, who have yet to win a World Series since the franchise’s founding in 1969 are just one win away from ending that drought, and it appears as though Brewers fans have come from far and wide in the hopes of witnessing history.
 With World Series ticket prices for games 1 and 2 in Milwaukee surging through the roof, taking a trip to the Tampa Bay area – where prices have plummeted as the Rays appear to be dead in the water – might have provided a more cost-effective way to support their team.
 A LOUD ovation as the @Brewers take the field to warm up ahead of Game 4 pic.twitter.com/8H93xfEyD7 
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 27, 2026

 Tale of the tape on Game 4's starting pitchers
 By Kevin Dotson 
 Griffin Jax pitches for Tampa Bay during a playoff game against the New York Yankees earlier this month. 
 Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images 
 As the World Series reaches Game 4, both the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays are turning to lesser-used starting pitchers. Lesser-used primarily because each team reached the Fall Classic with such ease that neither had to dig too deeply into its pitching reserves.
 With a chance to close out the World Series, the Brewers are sending lanky, red-haired Dustin May to the mound. Though May is making just his second start in these playoffs, he’s no stranger to the biggest stage in baseball.
 In 2020, May started three games for the Los Angeles Dodgers in their championship run that culminated with a win over the Rays. With an ERA of 5.63 in the 2026 playoffs, the Brewers might need their high-octane offense to stay hot if they are going to hoist the Commissioner’s Trophy tonight.
 The Rays are pinning their hopes on Griffin Jax in their do-or-die game. Jax, making his second career postseason start, has been a serviceable starter for Tampa Bay this season after a career spent mostly pitching in relief.
 Jax, who has yet to take the mound in the World Series, has struggled in these playoffs, with an ERA of 6.00 in a pair of appearances in earlier series.

 They’re chasing a World Series. Their families are just trying to survive October
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Drew Rasmussen poses with his wife, Stevie, and their children, Miller and Rhett, during an All-Star event in July. 
 Rob Tringali/MLB Photos/Getty Images 
 Miller Rasmussen, the daughter of Rays’ ace Drew Rasmussen and his wife Stevie, was born during opening week of the 2026 MLB season.
 It was a difficult birth, with Miller needing to spend time in the NICU. As baseball was happening every day, Stevie felt like she was immediately in survival mode. She told herself, “Just get through the end of the season.”
 “Then the season’s like a little bit longer, and a little bit longer,” Stevie Rasmussen told CNN Sports .
 Their rental home in St. Petersburg, Florida, ran through September, so they had to move late last month. They had the option to lease the new place for two weeks or all of October – they opted for the full month.
 “So now I’m like, ‘OK, we’re here. We might as well win the whole thing,’” she said.
 Down 3-0 in the World Series to the Milwaukee Brewers, the Rays will need a historic comeback to win the whole thing, but they’ve already gone deeper into the postseason than most of their players have ever experienced, with their families along for the incredibly hectic ride.
 “My kids have no schedule, no nap routine,” Stevie Rasmussen said.
 Read more here on how baseball families survive this crazy month.
 Read more 
 Link Copied!
 Tropicana Field is World-Series-ready after being shuttered for the 2025 season
 By Kevin Dotson 
 The Brewers warm up at Tropicana Field before Game 3. 
 Mike Carlson/MLB Photos/Getty Images 
 The Rays are hosting their first World Series games since 2008, and their home stadium – the quirky Tropicana Field – is ready to meet the moment.
 This was no certainty heading into the 2026 season, after “The Trop” sustained significant damage from Hurricane Milton in October 2024. The domed stadium’s fabric roof was ripped to shreds by the powerful winds of the storm.
 The Rays spent the entire 2025 season playing their home games at cross-bay George M. Steinbrenner Field, the spring training home of the rival New York Yankees. And it was a race against the clock to get Tropicana Field ready for Opening Day this year.

 But here we are, six months later, and the Fall Classic has come to St. Petersburg, and Tropicana Field’s quirky architecture might be just what the Rays need to turn the momentum of this series. The roof of the Trop, which is nearly identical in color to a baseball and criss-crossed by a network of wires and catwalks – all of which are in play – has the potential to turn any game on its head.
 Depending on where a ball might strike the roof, it could result in an automatic home run or remain a live ball with the defensive players able to play the ball wherever it falls.
 For anyone new to Tampa Bay Rays baseball, buckle up and expect the unexpected.

 Aaron Ashby is closing out games with deep breaths and scoreless frames
 By Hannah Keyser 
 Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby pitches during Game 1 of the World Series. 
 Stacy Revere/Getty Images 
 Before this year, Aaron Ashby was not a very good postseason pitcher.
 The bespectacled lefty had thrown just over nine playoff innings and allowed nine runs. But right now he is on the verge of historical dominance that has helped power the Brewers to being just two wins away from their first championship.
 His 15 ⅔ scoreless innings is one out away from matching the record set by Andrew Miller in 2016 for the longest scoreless streak of relief innings in a single postseason.
 That may sound like a lot of conditions but it reflects a very simple fact: Ashby hasn’t allowed anything
 this October. Every time Brewers manager Pat Murphy calls for him out of the pen, Ashby delivers a zero.
 After closing out Game 2, he said that his failures in previous postseason have taught him how to stay calm.
 “Trying to grip it too tight and make too much happen, be too good, throw too hard, any number of things that you can do in big situations when there’s a lot of adrenaline,” Ashby said. “So, trying something new, I guess.”
 This time around, however, “A lot of breathing, just kind of praying for peace,” Ashby said.
 That and believing in his backstop.
 “He is in control right now,” Ashby said of William Contreras. “I feel like I’m just trusting him. There’s not a lot of thinking I got to do.”
